chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
title: The duet's place in jazz history; first bass and saxophone duo
summary: Crouch calls it one of the great jazz duets; Stewart had never seen a saxophone and bass play alone and was nervous without accompaniment.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Well, yes, they are. I mean, it's considered by the critical establishment in jazz one of the great duets ever recorded. There's King Oliver and Jelly Roll Morton. There's Louie Armstrong and Earl Hines. There's you and Don Byas and there's a couple others. But I mean, in the list of the great jazz duets, that's one of them that's always mentioned. It's never mentioned that they talk about the great duets in jazz that that's not one of them.
Oh, and a couple of them that Blanton and Ellington did. But I mean, whichever ones they talk about, that's one of the ones that they say is one of the greatest ever recorded.
But now, at that time, was there ever -- had you, outside of a jam situation, had you ever seen a saxophonist and a bassist perform?
That way, just two of us, you know.
No, I haven't. I'd never noticed it until we did it, you know.
That was the first time you ever saw that happen.
Yeah, that's the reason why I said in front, I was very disturbed by the fact that we wouldn't have any accompanist like piano or a drummer or what have you.
Guitar or something like that, you know.
